ican.text: I can identify a sector’s radius, central angle, arc and perimeter.
I can find an arc length or sector area using a central angle measured in degrees.
I can solve for an unknown radius or central angle from an arc length or sector area.
I can distinguish a sector from a segment and account for all boundaries when finding perimeter.
I can apply the formulas to a context, use suitable units and check my result against the whole circle.

ku.text: A sector is the region bounded by two radii and the arc joining their endpoints. Its central angle is measured at the centre of the circle; the arc is only the curved part of its boundary.

If the central angle is $\theta^\circ$, the sector occupies a fraction $\theta/360$ of a full circle. For a radius $r$, arc length is $s=\frac{\theta}{360}(2\pi r)$ and sector area is $A=\frac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2$.

The same fraction applies to circumference and area for the same angle, but circumference is proportional to $r$ whereas area is proportional to $r^2$. Arc length has length units and area has square units.
The perimeter of an ordinary sector includes its arc and two radii: $P=s+2r$. A question about a curved boundary alone asks for $s$, not the whole sector perimeter.
When given an arc length and radius, rearrange to $\theta=\frac{360s}{2\pi r}$. When given sector area and radius, use $\theta=\frac{360A}{\pi r^2}$. The resulting angle is in degrees.

A segment is bounded by a chord and an arc. For a minor segment, subtract the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and chord from the corresponding minor-sector area. The triangle area is $\frac12r^2\sin\theta$ for $0^\circ<\theta<180^\circ$.
For a major sector, use the specified reflex central angle or subtract the minor-sector measure from the whole circle. Check that a major sector occupies more than half the circle.

Radians are not required for SL 3.4 in the local syllabus. If using $s=r\theta$ or $A=\frac12r^2\theta$, the numerical value of $\theta$ must be in radians; the degree formulas above avoid that conversion.
Check that the chosen angle matches the region, all measurements use compatible units and the result is less than the full circumference or full area for a sector smaller than a full turn.

misc.weak: The perimeter of the sector is just its arc length.
misc.better: For the full sector boundary, add both radii: $P=s+2r$.

misc.weak: Use the diameter as $r$ in the sector formula.
misc.better: The radius is half the diameter. Convert before applying the formula.
The full-circle area is $\pi r^2$, so multiply that by the sector fraction.

misc.weak: A central angle of $240^\circ$ gives the minor sector.
misc.better: It gives the major sector. The other central angle is $120^\circ$.
That formula needs radians. In degrees, use $s=\frac{150}{360}(2\pi r)$.

misc.weak: A sector and a segment are the same region.
misc.better: A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc. A segment is bounded by a chord and an arc.

terms.text: An angle whose vertex is at the centre of the circle.
A portion of the circle’s circumference.
The region between two radii and their connecting arc.
A line segment joining two points on a circle.
A region bounded by a chord and the corresponding arc.
The total length around the stated region, including straight and curved boundaries.

formula.text: For a central angle $\theta$ measured in degrees: $s=\frac{\theta}{360}(2\pi r)$ and $A=\frac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2$.
For a sector bounded by two radii and the arc, $P=2r+s$.
For a minor segment with central angle $\theta$, subtract the triangle area $\frac12r^2\sin\theta$ from the sector area.

worked.prompt: A circular garden has centre $O$ and radius $12$ m. Two straight paths run along radii $OA$ and $OB$, forming a minor central angle $\angle AOB=150^\circ$. The region between the two radii and the minor arc is planted with flowers.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the exact length of the minor arc $AB$ and its value to three significant figures.
parts.a: The sector fraction is $150/360=5/12$. Thus $s=\frac5{12}(2\pi)(12)=10\pi$ m $\approx31.4$ m.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find the area of the flower sector and the length of its full perimeter.
parts.a: $A=\frac5{12}\pi(12)^2=60\pi\text{ m}^2\approx188\text{ m}^2$. The boundary consists of the arc and both radii, so $P=10\pi+24$ m $\approx55.4$ m.

parts.label: c
parts.q: A straight chord joins $A$ and $B$. Find the area between this chord and the minor arc.
parts.a: Triangle $AOB$ has area $\frac12(12)(12)\sin150^\circ=36\text{ m}^2$. The minor segment area is therefore $60\pi-36\text{ m}^2\approx152\text{ m}^2$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Find the area of the rest of the circular garden, outside the flower sector.
parts.a: The full circle has area $144\pi\text{ m}^2$. Subtract the flower sector: $144\pi-60\pi=84\pi\text{ m}^2\approx264\text{ m}^2$.

parts.label: e
parts.q: A second sector with the same radius has an arc length of $8\pi$ m. Find its central angle in degrees.
parts.a: Set $8\pi=\frac{\theta}{360}(24\pi)$. The arc is one third of the full circumference, so $\theta=120^\circ$.

kq.q: Why do the degree formulas use the fraction $\theta/360$?
kq.model: Equal central angles divide a circle into equal proportions. A sector with angle $\theta$ occupies $\theta/360$ of the full turn, circumference and area.

kq.q: Why does sector perimeter include more than the arc?
kq.model: The region’s boundary also includes the two straight radii that connect the arc endpoints to the centre.

kq.q: How can the area of a minor circular segment be found?
kq.model: Subtract the area of the triangle between the two radii and the chord from the area of the matching minor sector.

kq.q: Why does doubling the radius quadruple sector area for a fixed angle?
kq.model: The sector fraction stays fixed, while the whole-circle area contains $r^2$. Doubling $r$ multiplies the area by four.
